subject: Business Models
title: Standard Oil and Monopoly
description: A 60-second lesson on Standard Oil and Monopoly.

hook.text: John D. Rockefeller controlled 90% of American oil refining by 1880. One man, one industry.

buildup.text: He undercut competitors on price, bought them out, and controlled railroads to lock them out.

discovery.text: Standard Oil's prices were actually lower for consumers. Monopoly delivered efficiency—at a cost.

twist.text: In 1911, the Supreme Court broke Standard Oil into 34 companies. Some became Exxon, Mobil, Chevron.

climax.text: The breakup proved antitrust works: competition returned and innovation flourished.

punchline.text: One oil company became 34. Competition won.

quiz.question: What percentage of US oil refining did Standard Oil control?

details.summary: John D. Rockefeller built Standard Oil into a monopoly controlling 90 percent of US oil refining through aggressive acquisitions, railroad rebate deals, and predatory pricing. The company's dominance led to the 1911 Supreme Court antitrust ruling that broke it into 34 separate companies.
details.whyItMatters: Standard Oil defined the modern concept of monopoly and triggered the antitrust movement that still shapes business regulation. Its breakup created companies that became ExxonMobil, Chevron, and other oil giants, each worth tens of billions..
takeaways: Standard Oil controlled 90 percent of US oil refining through acquisitions and deals
Predatory pricing and railroad rebates eliminated competitors systematically
The 1911 breakup created 34 companies including predecessors of ExxonMobil and Chevron

faq.question: How did Standard Oil achieve monopoly control?
faq.answer: Rockefeller negotiated secret railroad rebates that undercut competitors' shipping costs. He bought competitors at depressed prices or drove them out through predatory pricing. Vertical integration from wells to retail gave cost advantages at every level..

faq.question: What was the impact of Standard Oil's breakup?
faq.answer: The 34 successor companies competed against each other, driving innovation and efficiency. Ironically, the total value of the broken-up pieces far exceeded the whole. The ruling established the precedent that market power achieved through anticompetitive practices violates the Sherman Antitrust Act.
